summary: Unreal Engine is Epic Games' source-available real-time engine. Important correction to this project's subject record: version 6 has not shipped. On 17 June 2026 Epic released Unreal Engine 5.8 and, the same day, announced the plan for version 6; Epic's own documentation site carries 5.8 release notes and no version 6 documentation, and the community forum announcement dates the 5.8 release to that day. Everything below is scored against 5.8, the shipping engine. Verse is likewise not the gameplay language of the shipping engine: Epic documents Verse only under Fortnite and the Unreal Editor for Fortnite, and the 5.8 experimental feature list names no Verse or Scene Graph entry. In shipping Unreal the gameplay languages are Blueprint and C++. Epic's stated plan is to move the gameplay model to Verse for version 6, with early access targeted for the end of 2027, so a standards audience should treat Verse today as a language you can only run inside Epic's own Fortnite service, not as a portable engine feature. What the engine covers very well: rendering, geometry, physics, sound, packaging and, unusually, an open standard for immersive sessions, because head-mounted display support goes through the OpenXR plugin. What it does not cover is portability. The renderer's virtualized geometry system uses, in Epic's own words, an internal mesh format; the lighting system is an engine-private algorithm; and the built-in networking is the deepest lock-in of all, because replication is welded to the engine's own object model, its own wire protocol and matching client and server builds. The trap for a standards group is that almost every capability here is present and strong, and almost none of it is specified anywhere a second implementation could follow. The three places Unreal genuinely meets the outside world are OpenXR for sessions, the glTF importer and exporter for models, and Pixel Streaming, which sends rendered frames and sound to a plain web browser over WebRTC and so lets a cloud-rendered topology reach clients that could never run the engine.

coverage.note: The engine ships deferred and forward rendering paths for desktop and for head-mounted displays, plus a separate mobile path; the pass structure and render graph are engine-internal and are not published as anything a second implementation could follow.

coverage.note: The augmented reality module is part of the engine, not a plug-in. One switch on the session settings makes the system generate mesh data from tracked geometry that can be used for rendering, collision and navigation, with further switches for collision, navigation mesh and wireframe drawing. The geometry arrives as a tracked mesh object the game can query.

coverage.note: Classification exists but only as a point query: a mesh geometry can be asked what class of object sits at a world location, returning one value and the place it was measured. coverage.note: A navigation mesh is generated from the level's own collision geometry inside a bounds volume the author places, stored in the level as a RecastNavMesh actor and tiled so parts of it can be rebuilt. The walkable surface is therefore authored and carried with the level rather than recomputed by whoever opens it — inside Unreal. Nothing of it survives export to another engine or a neutral format, and arrival points are the project's own actors.

Unreal can georeference a level so its origin sits at a known place on Earth. It declares no map of a place with a version and a lifecycle, and publishes no transform between two maps.
The engine states no area over which anything applies; a georeferenced level is content placed on Earth, not a service declaring where it answers.

coverage.note: Unreal Engine's Level Streaming and World Partition load sub-levels with their own actors, blueprints, and gameplay into a persistent world. Data Layers can swap content by event. Sub-levels run their own logic. But there is no formal containment boundary protocol — no event propagation or consumption rule defining how a contained experience's messages interact with the host's.

coverage.note: Unreal Engine's replication system synchronises state within a single game session between server and clients. Cross-world coupling — where one Unreal world mutates another's state with nobody connected — is not a built-in capability. The engine's networking assumes a single authoritative server with connected clients.
